newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Stanbic H1 seen up despite bottler's debts.
newsitem.headline: Stanbic H1 seen up despite bottler's debts.

text.p: The 230 million rand owed by insolvent South African Pepsi bottler New Age Beverages (NAB) to Standard Bank Investment Corp (Stanbic) is expected to take the shine off the bank's otherwise healthy half-year earnings growth.

Analysts said on Friday that a robust increase in assets and fatter margins at Stanbic, which had been expected to lift its earnings around 20 percent, will be offset by much higher provisions to cover its exposure to the drinks firm.
"(NAB) will definitely have an effect on earnings. Stanbic will have to provide more against that large exposure...," said Mark Young, director of banking at ratings agency IBCA.
Stanbic is due to report results for the six months to end-June next Tuesday.

Standard Corporate and Merchant Bank head Jacko Maree said at the time of NAB's collapse in May that although the 230 million rand debt was "substantial", he did not believe it would have a material negative impact on group earnings.
Just three years after it spearheaded Pepsi's high-profile return to South Africa, NAB, which kicked off a South African version of the global cola wars, applied for voluntary liquidation.

Les Cohen of Westrust (Pty) Ltd, one of the three joint provisional liquidators, said on Friday that NAB was being wound up and creditors would be consulted. "(Stanbic) will recoup some of their losses...but it is impossible to know yet how much," he said.
Analysts polled by Reuters forecast Stanbic's headline interim earnings would rise to between 688.0 and 725.0 cents with the consensus at 704.3, a 17.0 percent rise from 602.0 cents a year ago.
They expected the dividend to be in a range of 127.5-132.0 cents, averaging out at 130.0 cents, from 109.0 last time.

Some analysts said a lower contribution from associate Liberty Life Association of South Africa Ltd would also hem in Stanbic's profits as the financial services giant reported from a very high earnings base.
Twelve-month earnings last year saw Stanbic's associate income soar to 222 million rand because Liberty changed the valuation of its life fund.

Analysts said factors in the bank's favour over the last six months included growth in offshore earnings, an expected 18.0 percent increase in advances and slightly wider margins due to the abolition of the financial services levy in October last year.
